questions.question: A linear program $\max\ \boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ has an optimal corner point, and $\boldsymbol{p}$ is a feasible corner point that is not optimal. Which statement about the corner points adjacent to $\boldsymbol{p}$ is guaranteed?
options: Every adjacent feasible corner point of $\boldsymbol{p}$ has a strictly larger value of $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$.
At least one adjacent feasible corner point of $\boldsymbol{p}$ is an optimal solution.
At least one adjacent feasible corner point of $\boldsymbol{p}$ has a strictly larger value of $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$.
Every adjacent corner point of $\boldsymbol{p}$ with a larger value of $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ is feasible.

questions.question: A linear program $\max\ \boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ has an optimal corner point. At the feasible corner point $\boldsymbol{p}$, no adjacent feasible corner point has a larger value of $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$. What follows about $\boldsymbol{p}$?
options: $\boldsymbol{p}$ is an optimal solution: no feasible point at all has a larger value of $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$.
$\boldsymbol{p}$ beats every feasible corner point, but a feasible point that is not a corner point may be better.
$\boldsymbol{p}$ is only best among its neighbours; the remaining corner points must still be compared with it.
$\boldsymbol{p}$ is optimal only if the feasible region of the linear program is also bounded.

questions.question: The result that a nonoptimal feasible corner point has a better adjacent feasible corner point is proved for $\max\ \boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$. How does it apply to a linear program $\min\ \boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ that has an optimal corner point?
options: Only when the feasible region is bounded, since replacing $\boldsymbol{c}$ by $-\boldsymbol{c}$ can make the program unbounded.
Better means a smaller value; apply the maximization result to $-\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ on the same feasible region.
Better still means a larger value of $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$, because the walk is defined for an increasing objective.
It needs a separate proof, because a minimum of $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ need not be attained at a corner point.

questions.question: A feasible corner point with no better adjacent feasible corner point is optimal when the linear program has an optimal corner point; this mirrors the fact that a local minimum of a convex function is a global minimum. What plays the role of the neighbourhood of a point in the linear-programming statement?
options: All feasible corner points of the linear program, compared at the same time.
All corner points, feasible or not, that share a binding constraint with it.
The corner points that are closest to it in Euclidean distance.
The feasible corner points that are adjacent to it.

questions.question: A linear program $\max\ \boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ has an optimal corner point. A walk starts at a feasible corner point and repeatedly moves to an adjacent feasible corner point with a strictly larger value of $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$. Why does the walk stop after finitely many moves?
options: Each move makes one more constraint binding, and the linear program has only finitely many constraints.
Each move at least halves the gap between the current value and the optimal value.
The value strictly increases, so no corner point is visited twice, and there are finitely many.
The feasible region is bounded, so a path along its edges has a finite total length.

questions.question: Maximize $Z=2x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq6$, $x_1\leq4$, $x_2\leq5$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$. A walk to better adjacent feasible corner points is at $(1,5)$, where $Z=7$; this corner lies on the boundary lines $x_1+x_2=6$ and $x_2=5$. What should the walk do next?
options: Stop: $(1,5)$ is optimal, since its adjacent feasible corner point $(0,5)$ has the smaller value $Z=5$.
Move to the adjacent feasible corner point $(4,2)$, where $Z=10$.
Move to $(6,0)$, where $x_1+x_2=6$ meets $x_2=0$ and $Z=12$.
Move to $(0,5)$, where $Z=5$, since a step down may open a better route.

questions.question: Maximize $Z=2x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq6$, $x_1\leq4$, $x_2\leq5$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$. Its feasible region is bounded. At the feasible corner point $(4,2)$, $Z=10$, and its adjacent feasible corner points are $(4,0)$ with $Z=8$ and $(1,5)$ with $Z=7$. Which conclusion is correct?
options: $(4,2)$ can only be called optimal after the other feasible corner points $(0,0)$ and $(0,5)$ have been evaluated too.
No conclusion is possible, since the walk must start at $(0,0)$ for its end point to be certified.
$(4,2)$ is not optimal, since $Z$ keeps growing along the line $x_1=4$ above $(4,2)$.
$(4,2)$ is optimal: an optimal corner point exists and no adjacent feasible corner point is better.

questions.question: A linear program $\max\ \boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ has an optimal corner point and exactly $7$ feasible corner points. A walk starts at one of them and moves each time to an adjacent feasible corner point with a strictly larger value of $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$. What upper bound on the number of moves follows from the strict increase?

Maximize $Z=x_1+2x_2$ subject to $2x_1+x_2\leq10$, $x_1+3x_2\leq15$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$. From the feasible corner point $(5,0)$ one moves along the line $2x_1+x_2=10$ in the direction $(-1,2)$, along which $Z$ increases. At which point does another constraint first become binding?

The result that every nonoptimal feasible corner point has a better adjacent feasible corner point assumes that the linear program has an optimal corner point. Which property of a linear program guarantees this assumption?
options: It has a feasible corner point, and its feasible region is a closed set.
It has an optimal solution, and its objective vector satisfies $\boldsymbol{c}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$.
It has a feasible corner point, and its objective is bounded on the feasible corner points.
It has a feasible corner point, and it has an optimal solution.

questions.question: In a proof, one moves from a nonoptimal feasible corner point $\boldsymbol{p}$ of $\max\ \boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ along a direction $\boldsymbol{u}$ with $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{u}>0$ that keeps $n-1$ linearly independent constraints binding, until another constraint binds. If an optimal corner point exists, why is such a constraint reached?
options: Otherwise all $\boldsymbol{p}+t\boldsymbol{u}$, $t\geq0$, are feasible and $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ is unbounded, so no optimum exists.
The feasible region is compact, so every ray starting at $\boldsymbol{p}$ leaves it after a finite step.
The $n-1$ binding constraints are linearly independent, so their line meets every other constraint boundary.
The value $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ rises along $\boldsymbol{u}$ until it reaches the optimal value, and the move stops there.

questions.question: A linear program $\max\ \boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ has an optimal corner point. A walk moves from a feasible corner point to an adjacent feasible corner point with a strictly larger value until no such neighbour exists. What holds when several adjacent feasible corner points are better?
options: The one with the largest increase must be taken, or the walk can stop at a nonoptimal corner point.
The choice can change the final value, so several walks have to be compared at the end.
Any of them may be taken, and every such walk ends at an optimal corner point.
The choice changes neither the final value nor the number of moves the walk needs.

questions.question: Maximize $Z=2x_1-x_2$ subject to $x_1-x_2\leq3$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$. Its feasible corner points are $(0,0)$ with $Z=0$ and $(3,0)$ with $Z=6$, and they are adjacent. Which statement about $(3,0)$ is correct?
options: It is optimal, since its only adjacent feasible corner point, $(0,0)$, has a smaller value of $Z$.
It is not optimal: the points $(3+t,t)$, $t\geq0$, are feasible with $Z=6+t$.
It is optimal, since it has the largest value of $Z$ among all feasible corner points.
It is not optimal: the points $(0,t)$, $t\geq0$, are feasible, and $Z$ grows along them.

questions.question: Maximize $Z=x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq4$, $x_1\leq3$, $x_2\leq3$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$. The feasible corner point $(3,1)$ has $Z=4$, and a walk finds that its two adjacent feasible corner points give $Z=3$ at $(3,0)$ and $Z=4$ at $(1,3)$. What does this tell us about optimal solutions?
options: $(3,1)$ is not optimal: the tie with $(1,3)$ shows that the walk has to continue to $(1,3)$.
$(3,1)$ is the unique optimal solution, since no adjacent feasible corner point is strictly better.
$(3,1)$ and $(1,3)$ are the only optimal solutions, since optima of a linear program lie at corner points.
$(3,1)$ is optimal, and so is every point of the segment from $(3,1)$ to $(1,3)$.

questions.question: Maximize $Z=3x_1-x_2+2x_3$ over the cube $0\leq x_i\leq1$, $i=1,2,3$, whose corner points are its eight vertices; two vertices are adjacent when they differ in exactly one coordinate. Starting at $(0,1,0)$, a walk always moves to the adjacent vertex with the largest $Z$, as long as that is better. Which path does it follow?

A linear program $\max\ \boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ need not have an optimal corner point. Let $\boldsymbol{p}$ be a feasible corner point. Which statement relating optimality of $\boldsymbol{p}$ to its adjacent feasible corner points holds for every such linear program?
options: $\boldsymbol{p}$ is optimal if and only if no adjacent feasible corner point has a larger value of $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$.
Having no better adjacent feasible corner point makes $\boldsymbol{p}$ optimal, while an optimal $\boldsymbol{p}$ may have a better neighbour.
If $\boldsymbol{p}$ is optimal, no adjacent feasible corner point is better, and if $\boldsymbol{p}$ is the best feasible corner point, it is optimal.
If $\boldsymbol{p}$ is optimal, none of its adjacent feasible corner points is better, but the converse can fail.

questions.question: A linear program $\max\ \boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ in $n$ variables has an optimal corner point, and $\boldsymbol{p}$ is a nonoptimal feasible corner point at which more than $n$ constraints are binding (a degenerate corner point). Which statement about better adjacent feasible corner points of $\boldsymbol{p}$ is correct?
options: The improving adjacent corner point theorem needs nondegeneracy, so $\boldsymbol{p}$ may have no better adjacent feasible corner point.
$\boldsymbol{p}$ still has a better adjacent feasible corner point, though some choices of $n$ binding constraints at $\boldsymbol{p}$ may not lead to it.
The better adjacent corner point may be $\boldsymbol{p}$ itself, described by another set of $n$ binding constraints.
If one choice of $n$ binding constraints at $\boldsymbol{p}$ leads to no better feasible corner point, $\boldsymbol{p}$ is optimal.

questions.question: Maximize the nonlinear function $f(x_1,x_2)=(x_1+4x_2-3)^2$ over the rectangle $R=[0,4]\times[0,1]$, whose corner points are $(0,0)$, $(4,0)$, $(4,1)$ and $(0,1)$. At $(0,0)$, $f=9$, and both adjacent corner points, $(4,0)$ and $(0,1)$, give $f=1$. Which statement is correct?
options: $(0,0)$ is a maximizer: $R$ is compact, so $f$ attains a maximum, and no adjacent corner point is better.
$(0,0)$ is a maximizer: it is a local maximum of $f$ on $R$, and $f$ is convex, so it is global.
$(0,0)$ is not a maximizer, as $f(4,1)=25$: the walk to better corners needs a linear objective.
No corner point maximizes $f$ on $R$, since $f$ is not linear, so its maximum lies inside an edge.

questions.question: Minimize $W=x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+2x_2\geq4$, $3x_1+x_2\geq6$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$; the feasible region is unbounded, with feasible corner points $(0,6)$, $(\frac{8}{5},\frac{6}{5})$ and $(4,0)$. At $(\frac{8}{5},\frac{6}{5})$, $W=\frac{14}{5}$, and both adjacent feasible corner points have larger $W$. What can be concluded?
options: $(\frac{8}{5},\frac{6}{5})$ is optimal: $W\geq0$ on the region, so an optimal corner point exists.
Nothing: on an unbounded region the result on better adjacent corner points never applies.
$(\frac{8}{5},\frac{6}{5})$ is not optimal: the region is unbounded, so $W$ is unbounded as well.
$(\frac{8}{5},\frac{6}{5})$ is best among corner points, but a point far out on a ray may give smaller $W$.
